Assume “cover a circle” means cover the filled disk of radius \(2\).

**1. Seven unit circles are enough.**

Place one unit circle at the center of the radius-\(2\) disk. Place six more unit circles with centers on a circle of radius \(\sqrt{3}\), equally spaced \(60^\circ\) apart.

Take any point \(P\) in the big disk.

- If its distance from the big center is \(\le 1\), it is covered by the central unit circle.
- Otherwise, its distance is \(r\) with \(1\le r\le 2\). By symmetry, \(P\) lies within \(30^\circ\) of one of the six outer centers \(C\). Let \(\theta\) be the angle between \(OP\) and \(OC\), so \(|\theta|\le 30^\circ\). Then

\[
PC^2=r^2+3-2\sqrt3\,r\cos\theta
\le r^2+3-3r
=1+(r-1)(r-2)\le 1.
\]

So \(P\) is inside that outer unit circle. Thus 7 circles cover the disk.

**2. Six unit circles are not enough.**

Suppose 6 unit circles cover the disk. Then their intersections with the boundary of the radius-\(2\) circle must cover the entire \(360^\circ\) circumference.

A unit circle has diameter \(2\). On a circle of radius \(2\), two boundary points more than \(60^\circ\) apart have chord length greater than \(2\), so they cannot both lie in the same unit circle. Therefore each unit circle can cover at most a \(60^\circ\) arc of the boundary.

Six arcs of length at most \(60^\circ\) can cover \(360^\circ\) only if each covers exactly \(60^\circ\). For an exact \(60^\circ\) arc, the endpoints are distance \(2\) apart, so the unit circle’s center must be the midpoint of that chord. In a radius-\(2\) circle, that midpoint is

\[
2\cos 30^\circ=\sqrt3
\]

from the big center. Hence all six centers would be distance \(\sqrt3>1\) from the big center, meaning the big center itself is not covered. Contradiction.

So at least 7 are required, and 7 suffice.

\[
\boxed{7}
\]
